highlights.content: # AI Infrastructure Spending Boom Puts These Four Hardware Stocks in the Spotlight ##### Key Elements ![AI Infrastructure Spending Boom Puts These Four Hardware Stocks in the Spotlight](https://img.biggo.com/W86IwkN5_rzHmTr3oqdTSa_RFevjNblbAx7c4COdpPA/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA4L2VlMDM2M2NiLWJmMDQtNDdmMi1hNzE4LWMyOGRjMWMwMDAwNF8xNzg3NDIzOTU5X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) The race to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure is accelerating at a breathtaking pace, with Alphabet and Amazon alone planning to pour roughly $420 billion into capital expenditures in 2026. That torrent of spending is flowing directly to a handful of hardware companies positioned to capture the lion's share of the AI build-out. Alphabet expects to spend between $195 billion and $205 billion this year, while Amazon has raised its 2026 spending target to approximately $220 billion, up from an earlier plan of $200 billion. The sheer scale of these commitments underscores how aggressively the hyperscalers are moving to expand cloud computing capacity in response to surging demand for AI workloads. For investors looking to ride this wave, the beneficiaries are increasingly concentrated in the semiconductor supply chain. Nvidia (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO), Micron Technology (MU), and Sandisk (SNDK) stand out as four hardware names directly levered to the AI capital expenditure cycle. **The Compute Leaders** Nvidia remains the most obvious beneficiary. Its data center GPUs have become the de facto standard for AI training and inference, and cloud computing clients continue to demand access to Nvidia hardware because it is universally recognized as best in class. The company has told investors it expects AI hyperscaler spending to top $1 trillion next year, suggesting the current boom is far from peaking. Broadcom occupies a complementary position in the ecosystem. The company has partnered with Alphabet to develop the Tensor Processing Unit, or TPU, a custom AI chip purpose-built for AI workloads. TPUs offer superior cost-performance compared to Nvidia's chips for certain workloads, though they require proper setup and can effectively lock clients into Alphabet's cloud ecosystem. With massive demand for TPUs on Alphabet's cloud platform, a meaningful portion of the search giant's roughly $200 billion in annual spending is expected to flow directly to Broadcom. Broadcom's custom AI semiconductor division is already generating significant revenue, with second-quarter sales of $10.8 billion. Management expects the division to deliver more than $100 billion in annual sales, highlighting the scale of the opportunity ahead. **The Memory Squeeze** While compute chips grab most of the headlines, the memory chip market is experiencing a supply crunch that is quietly reshaping the economics of the AI build-out. Memory prices have skyrocketed, and the shortage is severe enough that Amazon specifically cited higher memory costs as the reason it raised its 2026 spending plans from $200 billion to $220 billion. Micron and Sandisk, both major producers of memory chips, are benefiting enormously from these market conditions. In Sandisk's latest quarterly results, the company attributed one-third of its revenue growth to increased output and two-thirds to rising prices. The dynamic is straightforward: the memory chip market simply does not have enough capacity to meet the massive demand from AI hyperscalers, and when supply falls short of demand, prices soar. What makes this particularly attractive from an investor's perspective is that input costs for Micron and Sandisk are not rising in tandem. The profit windfall is flowing almost entirely to the bottom line as end selling prices climb. Micron's management team has indicated the shortage is expected to persist into 2028, suggesting there is still substantial room for memory prices to continue rising. **The Diversified Approach** For investors who prefer a broader approach...

News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The FTC Has Policed 13 AI Cases. None Target Agent Behavior. Operation AI Comply has recovered nearly $51 million from companies that lied about their AI tools. But deployed agents making real decisions remain outside the scope of federal enforcement. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| The Federal Trade Commission has initiated at least 13 enforcement actions since launching [Operation AI Comply](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/09/ftc-announces-crackdown-ai-enabled-scams-operation-ai-comply) in September 2024. Every one of these cases targets marketing deception—what is commonly called AI washing—rather than the actual behavior of the software. While the agency is aggressively policing the gap between vendor promises and tool capabilities, the internal mechanics of [autonomous agents](/glossary/ai-agent-security/) remain outside the scope of federal oversight. This focus on marketing claims is the primary axis of current federal enforcement. Settlements such as the $930,000 agreement with [CMG Media](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/05/ftc-takes-action-against-company-falsely-claiming-its-ai-tool-could-record-and-analyze-private-conversations) in May 2026 regarding a fictitious ‘Active Listening’ tool, and the $50 million settlement with [Growth Cave](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/01/ftc-charges-growth-cave-with-deceiving-consumers-about-ai-powered-business-coaching-tools) in January 2026, demonstrate a clear pattern. The agency is effectively policing the distance between a vendor’s claims and the software’s actual capabilities. However, this approach leaves the operational reality of autonomous agents largely untouched. The [Congressional Research Service](https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/IF/IF13151) confirmed in report IF13151, published July 6, 2026, that there is currently no federal guidance specifically addressing agentic AI. Although the [AI AGENT Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3565) was introduced as a discussion draft in June 2026 to establish a registration framework and designate the FTC as the principal authority for consumer-focused autonomous agents, it has not been enacted. Consequently, while the federal government is building a toolkit—including the March 2026 AI Policy Statement and proposed policies on [deceptive steering and personalized pricing](/the-ftcs-personalized-pricing-policy-targets-where-ai-meets-the-consumer-wallet/)—these tools have yet to be applied to the actual behavior of deployed agents. A regulatory divergence is emerging at the state level. In jurisdictions like Connecticut, Maryland, and New Jersey, state laws are beginning to capture autonomous agents through broad definitions of price-setting devices, as [our analysis of state surveillance pricing laws](/three-states-banned-agent-pricing-without-naming-agents/) details. This creates a fragmented environment where a company might be compliant with federal marketing standards while simultaneously running afoul of state-level operational requirements for algorithmic pricing. The tension between state AI regulation and federal preemption, [as seen in Colorado’s ADMT rulemaking](/colorado-is-writing-ai-transparency-rules-the-ftc-says-federal-law-may-override-them/), compounds this divergence. Advertisement This divergence is compounded by the FTC’s increasing use of the ‘means and instrumentalities’ doctrine. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Aug 23, 2026, 07:55 AM Updated Aug 23, 2026, 07:55 AM AI generated Some of Nvidia’s largest customers have been told prices of servers containing its AI chips will rise by more than 15 per cent in many cases with memory chip costs soaring, Bloomberg News reported on Aug 22. The price hikes will go into effect on systems shipped early 2027 and will impact systems including those with the flagship Vera Rubin and [Grace Blackwell chips](/business/nvidia-ceo-unveils-new-tech-to-keep-global-ai-expansion-going?ref=inline-article), the report added, citing people familiar with the process. The increases will depend on Nvidia’s chip generation and memory configurations, they said. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comments outside regular business hours. Companies that build servers under contract for large data centre operators such as Microsoft, Alphabet’s Google and Oracle have recently informed their customers of the upcoming increases, the report added. Nvidia, whose chips underpin much of the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, is set to report second-quarter results on Aug 26. The company has become a proxy for the [broader AI ecosystem](/business/companies-markets/nvidia-partners-wall-street-giants-to-raise-640-billion-for-ai-infrastructure?ref=inline-article) spanning chipmakers and companies financing the rapid expansion of data centre capacity. highlights.content: ![ChartMill Logo](assets/images/logo.png) ![Data Center and Cloud Infrastructure Earnings Face a High-Stakes AI Demand Test](https://www.chartmill.com/images/uploads/cloud_infrastructure_stocks_97f70d97a9.webp) # Data Center and Cloud Infrastructure Earnings Face a High-Stakes AI Demand Test ## Quotes Stocks Mentioned ### Article Mentions: The data center and cloud infrastructure theme is entering one of its most consequential earnings windows of the year. The group has delivered substantial gains over the past twelve months, powered by the buildout of AI compute capacity, yet the recent tape has turned uneven. With several of the sector's largest names reporting within days, the debate is no longer whether AI spending is happening, but whether it is happening fast enough to support the multiples already embedded in these stocks. ## The earnings gauntlet The broad theme's weighted performance over the past year is up roughly 30.4%, with six-month gains near 19.7%. The near-term picture is more fragile: the weighted average return over the last week is negative 3.0%. That disconnect matters. After a long run, investors are rotating toward selectivity, weighing high growth expectations against valuation discipline. The challenge was visible in the latest report from a major AI server vendor: earnings beat expectations, but a revenue shortfall cooled the reaction. It is a reminder that in this part of the market, the bar is no longer simply beating the consensus; it is beating it on the metrics that justify the next leg of capital spending. ## NVDA: chip demand sets the tone NVIDIA CORP ([NASDAQ:NVDA](https://www.chartmill.com/stock/quote/NVDA/profile)) is the sector's bellwether. Its report, due in four days, will effectively frame the earnings season for the entire theme, because its revenue and margins are the clearest signal of AI chip demand. Key figures: The market's willingness to look through the high trailing multiple rests on the assumption that demand stays at this pace. The stock fell 4.6% last week, a modest pullback relative to its 12-month gain, but the reaction to its upcoming numbers will likely set the tone for the group. ## MSFT: Azure and the enterprise AI test MICROSOFT CORP ([NASDAQ:MSFT](https://www.chartmill.com/stock/quote/MSFT/profile)) is the key read on enterprise AI adoption. Azure's growth trajectory is the main swing factor, and with a report due in five days, investors will look for confirmation that corporate customers are translating AI interest into committed cloud spending. Key figures: The stock is up 26.6% over the last month, making it the strongest near-term performer in this group. But the valuation leaves little room for error. Azure growth and any commentary on AI capacity constraints will be the metrics that matter. ## GOOGL: cloud momentum and margin leverage ALPHABET INC-CL A ([NASDAQ:GOOGL](https://www.chartmill.com/stock/quote/GOOGL/profile)) enters its report with the strongest relative strength in the group, outperforming 87.6% of the market. Google Cloud has become a genuine growth engine, and its profitability trajectory is central to the investment case. Key figures: The question for this report is not just growth, but the pace of margin expansion in Google Cloud. If the division continues to show operating leverage, the valuation case becomes easier to defend. ## AMZN: AWS and the cost of growth AMAZON.COM INC ([NASDAQ:AMZN](https://www.chartmill.com/stock/quote/AMZN/profile)) carries the most weight in the cloud infrastructure trade because AWS is the largest pure cloud platform. Its report, due in six days, offers the broadest view of enterprise demand and AI-related workloads. highlights.content: ![The Daily AI Digest logo](https://assets.buttondown.email/images/c8185e5c-50f4-4936-818d-19aa3b93251c.png) # [The Daily AI Digest](https://buttondown.com/dailyaidigest) # D.A.D.: Giving AI 'Memory' Can Make Its Answers Worse, Researchers Find — 8/22 AI Digest - 2026-08-22 # The Daily AI Digest Your daily briefing on AI August 22, 2026 · 10 items · ~5 min read From: DeepMind, Hacker News, NBER, arXiv D.A.D. Joke of the Day I asked AI to summarize the meeting. It gave me three action items, two next steps, and one thing that definitely wasn't said. ## What's New AI developments from the last 24 hours ### [A Phone App That Autocompletes Your Piano Playing—No Cloud Needed](https://simedw.com/2026/08/20/midi-autocomplete/?utm_source=dailyaidigest&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=dad-giving-ai-memory-can-make-its-answers-worse) A developer built RollTab, an iPhone/iPad app that autocompletes piano playing in real time as you play a MIDI keyboard, powered by a small AI model (125 million parameters, compact by industry standards) running entirely on the device rather than in the cloud. The breakthrough wasn't more computing power—it was rethinking how musical notes get encoded for the model. Early tokenization schemes needed over 16,000 tokens just for note on/off signals and caused notes to hang; a redesigned format tracking pitch, timing, duration, and velocity together fixed both speed and accuracy, hitting about 108 notes per second on an iPhone 15. **Why it matters:** It's a small-scale example of a bigger trend: clever data representation, not just bigger models, can make AI fast and capable enough to run offline on a phone. [Discuss on Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49373456&utm_source=dailyaidigest&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=dad-giving-ai-memory-can-make-its-answers-worse) · [Source: simedw.com](https://simedw.com/2026/08/20/midi-autocomplete/?utm_source=dailyaidigest&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=dad-giving-ai-memory-can-make-its-answers-worse) ### [Kagi Search Adds a One-Click Filter to Hide Paywalled Results](https://kagi.com/changelog?utm_source=dailyaidigest&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=dad-giving-ai-memory-can-make-its-answers-worse#11296) Search engine Kagi rolled out a changelog update on August 21 with a redesigned Stocks widget, tweaks to its Kagi Assistant chatbot, and a new toggle that automatically strips paywalled links out of search results. The paywall filter is opt-in, letting subscribers choose to see only freely accessible pages. One early commenter called it a "killer feature" and asked for a browser extension version. **Why it matters:** As more publishers wall off content, a one-click filter for free results is a small but telling sign that search tools are starting to compete on saving users time, not just finding links. [Discuss on Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49388154&utm_source=dailyaidigest&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=dad-giving-ai-memory-can-make-its-answers-worse) · [Source: kagi.com](https://kagi.com/changelog?utm_source=dailyaidigest&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=dad-giving-ai-memory-can-make-its-answers-worse#11296) ### [Traveler Reportedly Faces Felony After Phone Data Wiped at US Border](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/21/us/politics/samuel-tunick-deleted-phone-felony.html?utm_source=dailyaidigest&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=dad-giving-ai-memory-can-make-its-answers-worse) A US citizen reportedly faces a felony charge after phone data was erased during a US border inspection, according to a paywalled report. Details of the specific charge remain unclear. Community commenters speculate the traveler may have used a privacy-focused phone (GrapheneOS) with a "duress PIN"—a feature that wipes data if a specific code is entered, meaning the border officer, not the traveler, may have triggered the erasure. Others questioned whether prosecutors are pursuing a broader "obstruction" charge and suggested travelers use disposable phones when crossing borders...

highlights.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Rémi Louf: The CEO Who Fired Anthropic and Built a Better Agent Runtime in Two Weeks [Add to Google Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) When Rémi Louf, CEO of the 15-person AI firm .txt, tried to build an agent to handle his morning routine, he found the existing tools were less "autonomous robot" and more "tractor you still have to ride." Frustrated by frameworks that demand constant supervision and shocked by a 20% failure rate in Anthropic's structured outputs, Louf took two weeks off to build his own event-driven runtime from scratch. The result is a system running 20 production agents at .txt—some built by non-engineers—powered entirely by open-source models with zero third-party API spend. Louf's central argument is that the hard problems in agent orchestration are not new AI problems but old distributed-systems problems: durability, idempotency, and observability. His architecture rejects graph-based frameworks in favor of Markdown agent definitions, a causal event log, content-addressed prompts, and typed boundaries that make bad actions impossible. For investors and technologists watching the agent infrastructure boom, Louf's experience is a powerful data point: the framework category is unsettled, and a determined engineer with a clear philosophy can outperform venture-backed tooling in weeks. ##### Key Elements ![Rémi Louf: The CEO Who Fired Anthropic and Built a Better Agent Runtime in Two Weeks](https://img.biggo.com/N6NeuiCxQHGmG_ZOyta92uH8eSdVRRLZRud5f_50DC0/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA4L2U5ZWE4NTViN2E3NDkyOTdfMTc4NzQyNDM4MF9jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp) In December 2025, Rémi Louf decided that agentic AI had finally crossed a threshold. So the CEO of .txt, a 15-person AI company, did something unusual: he told his CTO he was going away, took two weeks off, and sat down to code. His goal was simple—a morning briefing assembled while he walked for an hour. What he found, he said on the AI Engineer podcast, was an industry selling the equivalent of a self-driving tractor mower that "you still have to stay on even if it's driving by itself. It can do many things, but you still have to be on." The tools on offer—a terminal interface you had to babysit, then an app he dismissed as "SSH with vibes"—all required him to steer from his phone mid-walk. So Louf stopped buying and started building. Two weeks later he had a working agent runtime. A month after that, .txt was running 20 production agents, some contributed by non-technical staff. And he had ripped out every third-party model API, replacing them with open-source models that run even on his laptop. His central claim is provocative: the hard parts of agent orchestration are not AI problems. They are the same distributed-systems problems software engineers have been solving for decades—durability, idempotency, observability, versioning. The frameworks promising to solve them with graphs and code abstractions are, in his view, the wrong layer. ### Every component exists because something broke Louf's architecture did not emerge from a whiteboard. It grew out of four real production failures in his first week. A daily brief posted to Slack twice. A voice note that vanished entirely. A market brief that turned into garbage after he edited a prompt. And, compounding that last failure, his realization that he had not versioned his prompt changes, so he could not reconstruct what he had altered. Each failure mapped to a fix. The vanished voice note produced a log. The duplicate Slack post produced a proper queue with attempt counting. The prompt regression produced a content-addressed system for prompt components. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The FTC Has Policed 13 AI Cases. None Target Agent Behavior. Operation AI Comply has recovered nearly $51 million from companies that lied about their AI tools. But deployed agents making real decisions remain outside the scope of federal enforcement. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| The Federal Trade Commission has initiated at least 13 enforcement actions since launching [Operation AI Comply](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/09/ftc-announces-crackdown-ai-enabled-scams-operation-ai-comply) in September 2024. Every one of these cases targets marketing deception—what is commonly called AI washing—rather than the actual behavior of the software. While the agency is aggressively policing the gap between vendor promises and tool capabilities, the internal mechanics of [autonomous agents](/glossary/ai-agent-security/) remain outside the scope of federal oversight. This focus on marketing claims is the primary axis of current federal enforcement. Settlements such as the $930,000 agreement with [CMG Media](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/05/ftc-takes-action-against-company-falsely-claiming-its-ai-tool-could-record-and-analyze-private-conversations) in May 2026 regarding a fictitious ‘Active Listening’ tool, and the $50 million settlement with [Growth Cave](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/01/ftc-charges-growth-cave-with-deceiving-consumers-about-ai-powered-business-coaching-tools) in January 2026, demonstrate a clear pattern. The agency is effectively policing the distance between a vendor’s claims and the software’s actual capabilities. However, this approach leaves the operational reality of autonomous agents largely untouched. The [Congressional Research Service](https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/IF/IF13151) confirmed in report IF13151, published July 6, 2026, that there is currently no federal guidance specifically addressing agentic AI. Although the [AI AGENT Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3565) was introduced as a discussion draft in June 2026 to establish a registration framework and designate the FTC as the principal authority for consumer-focused autonomous agents, it has not been enacted. Consequently, while the federal government is building a toolkit—including the March 2026 AI Policy Statement and proposed policies on [deceptive steering and personalized pricing](/the-ftcs-personalized-pricing-policy-targets-where-ai-meets-the-consumer-wallet/)—these tools have yet to be applied to the actual behavior of deployed agents. A regulatory divergence is emerging at the state level. In jurisdictions like Connecticut, Maryland, and New Jersey, state laws are beginning to capture autonomous agents through broad definitions of price-setting devices, as [our analysis of state surveillance pricing laws](/three-states-banned-agent-pricing-without-naming-agents/) details. This creates a fragmented environment where a company might be compliant with federal marketing standards while simultaneously running afoul of state-level operational requirements for algorithmic pricing. The tension between state AI regulation and federal preemption, [as seen in Colorado’s ADMT rulemaking](/colorado-is-writing-ai-transparency-rules-the-ftc-says-federal-law-may-override-them/), compounds this divergence. Advertisement This divergence is compounded by the FTC’s increasing use of the ‘means and instrumentalities’ doctrine. AI Agents.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/R1336Jyb-qk/hqdefault.jpg) [Half the Neoclouds WILL Die | Should we be fearful of Chinese Open-Source | Jerry Murdock](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R1336Jyb-qk) HostHarry StebbingsGuestJerry Murdock 5 hours ago01:09:58en ## Key Takeaways Venture capitalist Jerry Murdock warns that the AI bubble will burst between late October and March due to credit market complacency and geopolitical risks, and advises focusing investments on specialized applications and the model-agent-human layer rather than neoclouds or commodity infrastructure. ## Summary Jerry Murdock, co-founder of Insight Partners (managing over $90 billion), joins Harry Stebbings for a wide-ranging conversation that spans the AI bubble debate, credit market fragility, the frontier-versus-open-source model war, neocloud survival, AI security, and the coming shift to continuous-learning architectures. Murdock, who has invested through every major technology cycle of the past 25 years, delivers a distinctly contrarian take: the AI buildout is real and historically significant, but the current funding structure is dangerously dependent on debt that could crack under geopolitical stress. His central claim — that a sustained Iran conflict could trigger a credit dislocation that bursts the AI bubble between late October 2026 and March 2027 — frames the entire episode. The reader should walk away understanding that Murdock sees the AI opportunity as genuine but the current market structure as fragile, and that he believes the winners will be those who survive a coming shakeout, not those who are currently most visible. The conversation moves through several interlocking arguments. Murdock distinguishes between the underlying value of AI infrastructure — which he believes is permanent — and the financial engineering currently funding it, which he believes is precarious. He applies this lens to neoclouds (predicting at least half fail within 36 months), to the open-source versus frontier model competition (arguing specialization and customization will create a massive middle layer), and to the venture capital hype cycle (where he sees price sensitivity evaporating but discernment still rewarded). Throughout, he grounds his analysis in specific companies — Fireworks, Base 10, Cursor, Docker, E2B, OpenRouter, Aki Naki — and in his own investment philosophy, which prioritizes founders with no alternative but to build their companies. ## Credit market fragility and the AI bubble timeline Murdock's most provocative claim is a specific prediction: if the Iran war continues to fester, expect a correction, and depending on its depth, the AI bubble will burst between October 26, 2026 and March 2027. He draws a direct parallel to 2001 and 2008, when financial disruptions slowed innovation cycles that were otherwise real. The key difference this time, he argues, is debt — hyperscalers have taken on more debt than ever before, and neoclouds are even more exposed. > "If there is a dislocation, no one is better prepared to survive it than hyperscalers. Let's take neoclouds. I think at least half of them go away within 36 months." AI Agents.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Rémi Louf: The CEO Who Fired Anthropic and Built a Better Agent Runtime in Two Weeks [Add to Google Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) When Rémi Louf, CEO of the 15-person AI firm .txt, tried to build an agent to handle his morning routine, he found the existing tools were less "autonomous robot" and more "tractor you still have to ride." Frustrated by frameworks that demand constant supervision and shocked by a 20% failure rate in Anthropic's structured outputs, Louf took two weeks off to build his own event-driven runtime from scratch. The result is a system running 20 production agents at .txt—some built by non-engineers—powered entirely by open-source models with zero third-party API spend. Louf's central argument is that the hard problems in agent orchestration are not new AI problems but old distributed-systems problems: durability, idempotency, and observability. His architecture rejects graph-based frameworks in favor of Markdown agent definitions, a causal event log, content-addressed prompts, and typed boundaries that make bad actions impossible. For investors and technologists watching the agent infrastructure boom, Louf's experience is a powerful data point: the framework category is unsettled, and a determined engineer with a clear philosophy can outperform venture-backed tooling in weeks. ##### Key Elements ![Rémi Louf: The CEO Who Fired Anthropic and Built a Better Agent Runtime in Two Weeks](https://img.biggo.com/N6NeuiCxQHGmG_ZOyta92uH8eSdVRRLZRud5f_50DC0/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA4L2U5ZWE4NTViN2E3NDkyOTdfMTc4NzQyNDM4MF9jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp) In December 2025, Rémi Louf decided that agentic AI had finally crossed a threshold. So the CEO of .txt, a 15-person AI company, did something unusual: he told his CTO he was going away, took two weeks off, and sat down to code. His goal was simple—a morning briefing assembled while he walked for an hour. What he found, he said on the AI Engineer podcast, was an industry selling the equivalent of a self-driving tractor mower that "you still have to stay on even if it's driving by itself. It can do many things, but you still have to be on." The tools on offer—a terminal interface you had to babysit, then an app he dismissed as "SSH with vibes"—all required him to steer from his phone mid-walk. So Louf stopped buying and started building. Two weeks later he had a working agent runtime. A month after that, .txt was running 20 production agents, some contributed by non-technical staff. And he had ripped out every third-party model API, replacing them with open-source models that run even on his laptop. His central claim is provocative: the hard parts of agent orchestration are not AI problems. They are the same distributed-systems problems software engineers have been solving for decades—durability, idempotency, observability, versioning. The frameworks promising to solve them with graphs and code abstractions are, in his view, the wrong layer. ### Every component exists because something broke Louf's architecture did not emerge from a whiteboard. It grew out of four real production failures in his first week. A daily brief posted to Slack twice. A voice note that vanished entirely. A market brief that turned into garbage after he edited a prompt. And, compounding that last failure, his realization that he had not versioned his prompt changes, so he could not reconstruct what he had altered. Each failure mapped to a fix. The vanished voice note produced a log. The duplicate Slack post produced a proper queue with attempt counting. The prompt regression produced a content-addressed system for prompt components. The episode, published 2026-08-22, centers on a single, urgent claim: the AI takeover of human institutions is not a distant sci-fi scenario but a near-term probability, and the window to prevent it closes around the November 2028 US elections. Harari’s core argument is that the danger is not a Terminator-style rebellion but a quiet, voluntary surrender — humans will hand over finance, media, and even intimate relationships to AI systems because they are more efficient, more personalized, and increasingly more trusted than other humans. He frames the current moment as a choice, not a fate: “We are still in control in 2026, and it's our decision what to do now.” The conversation moves through four interlocking domains: the logical contradictions in Elon Musk’s public predictions, the mechanics of how trust migrates from humans to algorithms, the unprecedented ability of AI to mass-produce intimacy, and the specific regulatory asks Harari believes voters should demand from candidates in the upcoming midterms. The episode is dense with concrete provocations — from AI-generated fake lectures of Harari himself to the claim that money will disappear within a decade — and it ends with a clear, actionable framework for what politicians must address before it is too late. ## The Inevitability Narrative and Its Contradictions Harari opens by attacking the framing of inevitability that dominates AI discourse, using Elon Musk as his primary example. He argues that the “narrative of inevitability is a narrative of having no responsibility,” and that Musk’s own public statements are internally inconsistent. The critique is specific and pointed: * Musk predicts AI will take over the world in 10 years, yet simultaneously worries about Muslim immigration causing civil war in Britain in 20 years — a contradiction Harari calls out as nonsensical. * Musk predicts money will disappear in 10 years as AI takes over the financial system, yet he cut USAID funding to Africa to save money in the present. * Musk proposes government-issued checks to solve AI-driven mass unemployment, and when pressed on inflation, claims there will be deflation because AI will produce so much more. If that is true, Harari asks, why save money today at all? > “The narrative of inevitability is a narrative of having no responsibility.” The deeper point is that these contradictions reveal a refusal to engage with the present consequences of AI policy. Harari’s implicit argument: if the future is predetermined, then no one is accountable for the decisions made today. He rejects this, insisting that 2026 is still a moment of human agency. ## The Financial System: From Human Trust to Algorithmic Opacity Harari’s most developed argument concerns the financial system. He traces the history of money as a trust-building mechanism — from gold to paper to complex bonds — and notes that each innovation required humans to understand it at some level. All three ship weights you can download, fine-tune, and run on your own hardware, and all three sit within striking distance of GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5 on public leaderboards while costing a fraction as much per token. That combination is why “llama 4 maverick” alone pulls roughly 880 monthly US searches with low competition, and why engineering teams keep asking the same question: which of these three should actually run in production? This comparison breaks down the real numbers as of August 22, 2026: parameter counts, context windows, official pricing, published benchmark scores, self-hosting hardware requirements, and licensing terms. We also cover migration paths between the three, concrete use cases, and where each model falls short. Every figure below is sourced from official model pages, pricing trackers, or independent VRAM calculators current as of this month. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. None of these three is a universal winner. The right pick depends on whether you’re optimizing for licensing freedom, raw benchmark performance, ecosystem maturity, or self-hosting cost, and the rest of this article walks through each of those tradeoffs with the actual numbers. ## What are Llama 4 Maverick, Mistral Large 3, and DeepSeek V4-Pro? **Llama 4 Maverick** is Meta’s mid-tier model from the Llama 4 family, first released on April 5, 2025, and still the company’s most capable openly-licensed model as of August 2026 — Meta has not shipped a Llama 5 flagship yet. It uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with 400 billion total parameters routed across 128 experts, of which only 17 billion parameters activate per token. (Credit: Apple) Apple is the latest big tech firm to join the layoff spree affecting the industry. The Cupertino-based tech titan cut more than 200 employees from its Siri voice assistant, Vision Pro spatial computing headset, and broader artificial intelligence teams, *Bloomberg's Mark Gurman* reported. The reductions split roughly evenly: approximately 100 positions eliminated from the Vision Pro organisation and another 100 from Siri and related software teams. Apple confirmed the direction of the move in a statement, saying the cuts were made 'to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users.' 'While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also impact a limited number of existing roles. We are grateful to these team members for their contributions, and we are committed to supporting them throughout their transition, including opportunities to apply for other roles at Apple.' ## What the Vision Pro Cuts Actually Eliminated The Vision Pro, Apple's mixed-reality headset that launched in early 2024 at a starting price of $3,499, was positioned as the company's most ambitious new hardware category in years. The device runs visionOS, Apple's spatial operating system, and was marketed heavily on its ability to deliver immersive video experiences and high-end spatial gaming. Those are precisely the capabilities now being wound down, affecting about 100 roles within the division. The gaming team is being largely disbanded and the immersive video production unit significantly reduced. Apple is also scaling back its dedicated immersive content production operation, with plans to rely more heavily on third-party creators going forward. Producing immersive video content at the quality Apple demanded required significant internal resources, and the active user base for the Vision Pro never grew large enough to justify that overhead at scale. The headset, at its price point, remained a product for enthusiasts and enterprise customers rather than a mainstream consumer device. Apple has not signalled a full retreat from spatial computing. The company is reportedly considering a new Vision Pro model for release as early as 2028, and visionOS will continue to be developed, Bloomberg reported. Resources are being realigned toward other products in the pipeline rather than simply cut from the business. The platform continues, but the teams that built its signature experiences largely do not. ## Siri's Architectural Overhaul and the Workers It Left Behind Apple is rebuilding Siri on an entirely new technical architecture, one designed from the ground up to support more advanced, AI-powered capabilities. Share [Add us on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cryptobriefing.com "Add Crypto Briefing as your preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.") by [Editorial Team](https://cryptobriefing.com/team/editorial-team/) Microsoft just shipped a framework that tackles one of the more annoying problems in AI agent development: the gap between how you train an agent and how you actually deploy it. Agent Lightning v1.0, released on August 17, is an open-source reinforcement learning framework that lets AI agents learn within the same harness they already use in production. ## What harnessed agentic RL actually means The framework introduces a paradigm Microsoft calls “harnessed agentic RL.” In traditional reinforcement learning setups for AI agents, you typically need to reconstruct the agent’s entire interaction loop inside a training environment. Agent Lightning flips the script. The deploy-time harness, meaning the existing infrastructure that manages how an agent interacts with the world, continues to govern the entire interaction loop during training. The trainer component only observes sequences of requests and responses from the underlying large language model. It never touches the harness itself. In practical terms, this means developers can apply reinforcement learning to their agents with zero changes to pre-existing code, tools, context, control flow, or environments. The agent talks to what it thinks is a normal LLM endpoint, but behind the scenes, Agent Lightning has slotted in a proxy that captures everything the trainer needs. The entire core framework is roughly 3,500 lines of Python. Advertisement ## The benchmark results are hard to ignore Microsoft backed up the release with evaluation results on SWE-bench Verified, a benchmark that measures an AI agent’s ability to resolve real-world GitHub issues from popular open-source Python repositories. Using Agent Lightning’s RL training pipeline on the Qwen3.5-9B model, the team achieved a 14.6-point absolute improvement on SWE-bench Verified, pushing the model’s score from 41.8% to 56.4%. That jump came from only 6,000 training examples and what Microsoft described as modest computational resources. The release includes complete workflows, training scripts, and a reproducible pipeline specifically designed for coding agents. #...

Traditionally, consultants have acted as an external support system, called in to crunch the numbers, trim head count, or identify growth opportunities. Now, AI is reshaping what clients want from consultants and how work gets done, creating a new job profile that blurs the lines between tech and consulting. Instead of [generalist teams](https://www.businessinsider.com/consulting-industry-outlook-management-consultants-ai-hiring-job-cuts-2026-3) producing research and strategy decks, consultants are increasingly expected to provide something tangible: tools, systems, and holistic, ongoing support. The big firms aren't only advising on tech strategy, they're building and implementing it, often through multi-year transformation projects. To win that work, consulting firms are racing to position themselves as "AI-native." "The more they're perceived to be a technology firm, the more likely they are to win business," Fiona Czerniawska, CEO of Source Global, a consulting sector intelligence firm, told Business Insider. But the transformation raises a key question: Are these companies fundamentally changing what they do, or merely how they describe themselves? ## **The race to become AI-native** Looking back atthe top firms' actions and rhetoric over the past year makes clear just how central AI has become to the consulting business. "There is no doubt that our firm is a tech company that delivers now on audit, tax, and advisory services," Tim Walsh, CEO of KPMG US, told Business Insider's Dan DeFrancesco at the World Economic Forum in January. AI Product.title: Is Employee AI Use Creating Your Next Cybersecurity Risk?
AI Product.titleZh: Is Employee AI Use Creating Your Next Cybersecurity Risk?
AI Product.content: # Are Employees Creating Your Organisation’s Next AI Security Risk? [Next story](/za/about/newsroom/press-releases-za/blog/how-qr-code-phishing-can-slip-past-corporate-security-measures/) Artificial intelligence is moving quickly from experimentation to everyday business use. Employees are using AI assistants to write content, analyse information, automate tasks and solve technical problems. Developers are experimenting with AI agents and AI skills, while teams are connecting third-party tools and plugins to existing workflows. For businesses, this creates a new question that goes beyond whether employees *should* use AI. ### Do You Have a Grip on What Your Employees Are Doing With AI? ESET's latest research suggests this question deserves closer attention. In H1 2026, ESET analysed nearly 900,000 AI skills from popular repositories, identifying 25,000 suspicious skills and more than 3,000 malicious instances. Some malicious skills incorporated hacking tools such as Mimikatz and Impacket, while others were capable of creating persistence mechanisms. ESET also identified seemingly legitimate but ineffective security skills that could create a false sense of protection. These findings highlight an important development in AI cybersecurity: the emerging AI ecosystem itself is becoming part of the enterprise attack surface. ### AI Adoption Is Creating A New Enterprise Attack Surface The conversation around AI risks in business has often centred on familiar concerns: sensitive information being entered into public AI tools, inaccurate AI-generated content or employees using unauthorised applications. Those concerns remain important. But the security picture is becoming more complicated. Today's Enterprise AI environment can include: * AI assistants and chatbots * AI-powered applications * Third-party plugins and integrations * AI skills that extend an agent's capabilities * Autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents * Developer tools and coding assistants * Custom AI workflows * AI services connected to business data and applications Each additional tool or capability can introduce new permissions, dependencies and potential points of compromise. This is why organisations need to start thinking about the AI attack surface for businesses in broader terms. It isn't simply about which AI platform employees are using. It is also about what those platforms can access, what they are allowed to do and what additional capabilities employees are installing or connecting to them. ### The Employee Isn't The Threat. The Lack Of Visibility Can Be. Employees are adopting AI tools because they can make everyday tasks faster and more efficient. Preventing AI use altogether is unlikely to be practical or desirable. The greater concern is unmanaged adoption. An employee might introduce an AI tool, a developer could install an AI skill, or a team might connect an AI service to a business application without security teams having visibility into the associated risks. To understand how employees using AI affect cybersecurity, rather than asking, *"Are our employees using AI?"* It should be "What AI are they using, what can it access, and what can it do?" ### AI Skills: Small Components, Potentially Significant Consequences [ESET's H1 2026 research](https://www.eset.com/za/business/threat-report/) provides an important example of why this matters. Between March and May 2026, ESET analysed approximately 900,000 AI skills from popular repositories. Of these, 25,000 were considered suspicious, and more than 3,000 were identified as malicious. AI skills can extend the functionality of an AI agent, allowing it to perform additional tasks. [Next story](/za/about/newsroom/press-releases-za/blog/how-qr-code-phishing-can-slip-past-corporate-security-measures/) Artificial intelligence is moving quickly from experimentation to everyday business use. Employees are using AI assistants to write content, analyse information, automate tasks and solve technical problems. Developers are experimenting with AI agents and AI skills, while teams are connecting third-party tools and plugins to existing workflows. For businesses, this creates a new question that goes beyond whether employees *should* use AI. ### Do You Have a Grip on What Your Employees Are Doing With AI? ESET's latest research suggests this question deserves closer attention. In H1 2026, ESET analysed nearly 900,000 AI skills from popular repositories, identifying 25,000 suspicious skills and more than 3,000 malicious instances. Some malicious skills incorporated hacking tools such as Mimikatz and Impacket, while others were capable of creating persistence mechanisms. ESET also identified seemingly legitimate but ineffective security skills that could create a false sense of protection. These findings highlight an important development in AI cybersecurity: the emerging AI ecosystem itself is becoming part of the enterprise attack surface. ### AI Adoption Is Creating A New Enterprise Attack Surface The conversation around AI risks in business has often centred on familiar concerns: sensitive information being entered into public AI tools, inaccurate AI-generated content or employees using unauthorised applications. Those concerns remain important. But the security picture is becoming more complicated. Today's Enterprise AI environment can include: * AI assistants and chatbots * AI-powered applications * Third-party plugins and integrations * AI skills that extend an agent's capabilities * Autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents * Developer tools and coding assistants * Custom AI workflows * AI services connected to business data and applications Each additional tool or capability can introduce new permissions, dependencies and potential points of compromise. This is why organisations need to start thinking about the AI attack surface for businesses in broader terms. It isn't simply about which AI platform employees are using. It is also about what those platforms can access, what they are allowed to do and what additional capabilities employees are installing or connecting to them. ### The Employee Isn't The Threat. The Lack Of Visibility Can Be. Employees are adopting AI tools because they can make everyday tasks faster and more efficient. Preventing AI use altogether is unlikely to be practical or desirable. The greater concern is unmanaged adoption. An employee might introduce an AI tool, a developer could install an AI skill, or a team might connect an AI service to a business application without security teams having visibility into the associated risks. To understand how employees using AI affect cybersecurity, rather than asking, *"Are our employees using AI?"* It should be "What AI are they using, what can it access, and what can it do?" ### AI Skills: Small Components, Potentially Significant Consequences [ESET's H1 2026 research](https://www.eset.com/za/business/threat-report/) provides an important example of why this matters. Share [Add us on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cryptobriefing.com "Add Crypto Briefing as your preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.") by [Editorial Team](https://cryptobriefing.com/team/editorial-team/) Microsoft just shipped a framework that tackles one of the more annoying problems in AI agent development: the gap between how you train an agent and how you actually deploy it. Agent Lightning v1.0, released on August 17, is an open-source reinforcement learning framework that lets AI agents learn within the same harness they already use in production. ## What harnessed agentic RL actually means The framework introduces a paradigm Microsoft calls “harnessed agentic RL.” In traditional reinforcement learning setups for AI agents, you typically need to reconstruct the agent’s entire interaction loop inside a training environment. Agent Lightning flips the script. The deploy-time harness, meaning the existing infrastructure that manages how an agent interacts with the world, continues to govern the entire interaction loop during training. The trainer component only observes sequences of requests and responses from the underlying large language model. It never touches the harness itself. In practical terms, this means developers can apply reinforcement learning to their agents with zero changes to pre-existing code, tools, context, control flow, or environments. The agent talks to what it thinks is a normal LLM endpoint, but behind the scenes, Agent Lightning has slotted in a proxy that captures everything the trainer needs. The entire core framework is roughly 3,500 lines of Python. Advertisement ## The benchmark results are hard to ignore Microsoft backed up the release with evaluation results on SWE-bench Verified, a benchmark that measures an AI agent’s ability to resolve real-world GitHub issues from popular open-source Python repositories. Using Agent Lightning’s RL training pipeline on the Qwen3.5-9B model, the team achieved a 14.6-point absolute improvement on SWE-bench Verified, pushing the model’s score from 41.8% to 56.4%. That jump came from only 6,000 training examples and what Microsoft described as modest computational resources. Infra & Chips.content: # AI Infrastructure Spending Boom Puts These Four Hardware Stocks in the Spotlight ##### Key Elements ![AI Infrastructure Spending Boom Puts These Four Hardware Stocks in the Spotlight](https://img.biggo.com/W86IwkN5_rzHmTr3oqdTSa_RFevjNblbAx7c4COdpPA/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA4L2VlMDM2M2NiLWJmMDQtNDdmMi1hNzE4LWMyOGRjMWMwMDAwNF8xNzg3NDIzOTU5X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) The race to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure is accelerating at a breathtaking pace, with Alphabet and Amazon alone planning to pour roughly $420 billion into capital expenditures in 2026. That torrent of spending is flowing directly to a handful of hardware companies positioned to capture the lion's share of the AI build-out. Alphabet expects to spend between $195 billion and $205 billion this year, while Amazon has raised its 2026 spending target to approximately $220 billion, up from an earlier plan of $200 billion. The sheer scale of these commitments underscores how aggressively the hyperscalers are moving to expand cloud computing capacity in response to surging demand for AI workloads. For investors looking to ride this wave, the beneficiaries are increasingly concentrated in the semiconductor supply chain. Nvidia (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO), Micron Technology (MU), and Sandisk (SNDK) stand out as four hardware names directly levered to the AI capital expenditure cycle. **The Compute Leaders** Nvidia remains the most obvious beneficiary. Its data center GPUs have become the de facto standard for AI training and inference, and cloud computing clients continue to demand access to Nvidia hardware because it is universally recognized as best in class. The company has told investors it expects AI hyperscaler spending to top $1 trillion next year, suggesting the current boom is far from peaking. Broadcom occupies a complementary position in the ecosystem. The company has partnered with Alphabet to develop the Tensor Processing Unit, or TPU, a custom AI chip purpose-built for AI workloads. TPUs offer superior cost-performance compared to Nvidia's chips for certain workloads, though they require proper setup and can effectively lock clients into Alphabet's cloud ecosystem. With massive demand for TPUs on Alphabet's cloud platform, a meaningful portion of the search giant's roughly $200 billion in annual spending is expected to flow directly to Broadcom. Broadcom's custom AI semiconductor division is already generating significant revenue, with second-quarter sales of $10.8 billion. Management expects the division to deliver more than $100 billion in annual sales, highlighting the scale of the opportunity ahead. **The Memory Squeeze** While compute chips grab most of the headlines, the memory chip market is experiencing a supply crunch that is quietly reshaping the economics of the AI build-out. Memory prices have skyrocketed, and the shortage is severe enough that Amazon specifically cited higher memory costs as the reason it raised its 2026 spending plans from $200 billion to $220 billion. Micron and Sandisk, both major producers of memory chips, are benefiting enormously from these market conditions. In Sandisk's latest quarterly results, the company attributed one-third of its revenue growth to increased output and two-thirds to rising prices. What makes this particularly attractive from an investor's perspective is that input costs for Micron and Sandisk are not rising in tandem. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Aug 23, 2026, 07:55 AM Updated Aug 23, 2026, 07:55 AM AI generated Some of Nvidia’s largest customers have been told prices of servers containing its AI chips will rise by more than 15 per cent in many cases with memory chip costs soaring, Bloomberg News reported on Aug 22. The price hikes will go into effect on systems shipped early 2027 and will impact systems including those with the flagship Vera Rubin and [Grace Blackwell chips](/business/nvidia-ceo-unveils-new-tech-to-keep-global-ai-expansion-going?ref=inline-article), the report added, citing people familiar with the process. The increases will depend on Nvidia’s chip generation and memory configurations, they said. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comments outside regular business hours. Companies that build servers under contract for large data centre operators such as Microsoft, Alphabet’s Google and Oracle have recently informed their customers of the upcoming increases, the report added. Nvidia, whose chips underpin much of the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, is set to report second-quarter results on Aug 26. The company has become a proxy for the [broader AI ecosystem](/business/companies-markets/nvidia-partners-wall-street-giants-to-raise-640-billion-for-ai-infrastructure?ref=inline-article) spanning chipmakers and companies financing the rapid expansion of data centre capacity. The price increase affects complete server systems containing Nvidia's AI accelerators, not just the chips themselves. These systems typically include multiple GPUs, specialized networking gear, and cooling infrastructure designed to handle the intense computational loads of AI workloads. It remains the dominant chip company for AI model training, and that is unlikely to change. Most early foundational AI code was written using its CUDA software platform and optimized for its graphics processing units (GPUs), creating a wide moat in this arena. Meanwhile, Nvidia hasn't rested on its laurels. The company is a huge player in data center networking, which has formed the base for it to become a complete AI infrastructure player offering end-to-end rack-scale solutions designed for specific AI tasks. Anthropic recruits a Google TPU pioneer as the computing power empire shifts from a "GPU solo" to a "heterogeneous computing symphony." Anthropic PBC has hired Amir Salek, founder of Alphabet Inc.'s Google custom AI chip project, to join its compute team. In his new role, Salek will report to James Bradbury, having previously overseen Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) business. Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Anthropic PBC, a global leader in large AI models and AI applications, has hired Amir Salek, one of the core founders of Alphabet Inc.'s Google's customized AI chip project (specifically the Google TPU AI chips). This move comes as the world's premier artificial intelligence laboratory lays a crucial foundation for its full-scale entry into the self-developed AI semiconductor sector (also known as customized AI ASIC/XPU chips, with TPU representing this technological route). The AI company stated on Friday that Salek will join the AI computing team at Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI super platform. Prior to 2022, he was responsible for Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) business and helped Google design the first seven generations of TPU chips. In his new role, Salek will report directly to James Bradbury, Anthropic's Head of AI Compute. ![](https://record.moomoo.com/news-editor-imgs/20260822/public/17874039027936790280542.png?imageMogr2/quality/minsize/1/ignore-error/1/format/webp)Microsoft (MSFT.US), one of the U.S. tech giants, plans to soon launch its latest self-developed AI accelerator, Maia. Additionally, a new agreement between Google and fabless chip company Marvell Technology covers various customized chips, including AI accelerators, storage, and memory controllers. These developments highlight that the construction of AI computing infrastructure, led by AI application leaders and hyperscale cloud providers, is comprehensively upgrading from "collective procurement of NVIDIA GPUs" to a heterogeneous computing system featuring large-scale coordinated operation of NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, self-developed AI Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (AI ASICs)/XPUs, and CPUs/DPUs. As AI large model architectures stabilize and token call volumes across global industries exhibit exponential growth, high-concurrency AI inference workloads are increasingly suitable for cost reduction per token through customized chips. ![](https://record.moomoo.com/news-editor-imgs/20260822/public/17874039027936790280542.png?imageMogr2/quality/minsize/1/ignore-error/1/format/webp) In other words, AI training operator processes and those frontier AI workloads with the most complex architectures and fastest rate of change still heavily rely on AI GPU clusters. Frontier model pre-training, reinforcement learning, and rapidly evolving new operators remain more dependent on GPU programmability, the CUDA ecosystem, and NVLink/NVSwitch clustering capabilities. Meanwhile, large-scale AI inference workloads surrounding mature and open-source AI large models, Copilot, and AI Agents are increasingly suited for specialized self-developed AI chips. According to institutions such as Morgan Stanley and Wedbush Securities, which remain bullish on AI compute infrastructure investments, the seemingly boundless frontier of cutting-edge compute demand in the AI inference era—and the growing need for compute resources driven by AI agents—enables AI ASICs to emerge as a critical component of a second trillion-dollar compute ecosys...
